newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek bourse battered by settlement scandal.
newsitem.headline: Greek bourse battered by settlement scandal.

text.p: The Athens bourse, rocked to its foundations over the past week, fell sharply on Thursday in the first normal session since a securities settlement scandal shut down most operations for four days.
Brokers said the repercussions from the Delta Securities scandal would be far-reaching and would cast a shadow over the bourse for some time to come.
The bourse closed down 3.31 percent or 30.04 points at 878.38 after opening at 908.07. Turnover was moderate at 5.019 billion drachmas. There was a steady across-the-board sell-off.

"Market sentiment is not good. Retail and institutional investors were selling," a floor trader said. Reflecting the nervous atmosphere because of the unfolding Delta scandal, no brokers or fund managers wanted to be named.

"People are selling, which was to be expected, but it's not aggressive selling as yet. Problems surrounding settlement and auditing transactions must be clarified. People are waiting to see how far the Delta scandal will reach," said a fund manager.
The crisis erupted when Delta, a relatively small brokerage, tried to settle its account at the bourse's clearing house with 2.6 billion drachmas ($11 million) in bad cheques.

The 65-member Association of Athens Stock Exchange Members (SMEHA), angered by perceived inaction by authorities to probe the scandal, refused to trade and effectively closed the bourse for four days.

The revolt by SMEHA brokers appears to have put pressure on bourse officials to watch transactions closer. Authorities have ordered a two-day suspension of trade in four stocks linked to the Delta scandal.
Magrizos, Parnassos, Hellenic Sugar Industry and St George Mills were suspended from trading on Thursday and Friday, a bourse statement said.
"The suspension is not related to the companies or their financial situation but is to facilitate any possible checks being conducted on transactions in their shares to date," it said.
The national economy ministry has ordered an audit of 10 brokerages and many brokers have said they would like to know which firms were on the opposite side of the Delta trades.
Some brokers said the scandal had brought to the fore a battle for survival among the increasing number of brokerages in Athens limited market.
"When commissions were liberalised it became obvious that the Athens stock exchange could no longer provide enough income for 65 brokers," said ING Barings in a recent report.
The scandal has also highlighted notorious short-selling, which has cried out for regulation but authorities have proved slow to move and apparently happy to turn a blind eye.
Short selling developed into a way to boost turnover in a thin market, make fast money on the downside and even to break even on previous losses, brokers said.

Although no one has said so officially, many brokers suspect short-selling was part of the Delta scandal. Three senior Delta officials have been charged with fraud and the firm's accounts and assets have been frozen.

ING Barings said bourse authorities would have to come up with a way to avoid similar crises in future and the government appeared more determined to get tougher with brokers who fail to settle on time.
Part of the Delta scandal appears to be linked to brokers taking advantage of an overburdened settlement system which can take up to 40 days to clear instead of the regulated 72 hours.
That means that unscrupulous brokers can sell shares short and capitalise on the prolonged time interval before having to actually deliver the securities, brokers said.
But the mechanism for detecting brokers who are selling with continuous rollovers will be weak until book-entry settlement is introduced in early 1997, ING Barings said.
Most brokers said that a full investigation into the Delta scandal would lead to a better market and, eventually, return the bourse to a healthy, well-regulated way to raise capital.

"A war amid the brokerage community has started, a war that is bound to continue. Many reacted because they realised they were being taken advantage of, the system was being abused," another broker said.
He said it boils down to brokers deciding to fight it out for survival but the market may benefit from a thorough house cleaning as well. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4 ($1=237.6 Drachma)
